title: Michael, Gabriel and Raphael (29 September)
hook: three angels with names: the protector, the messenger and the healer

segments.voice: Yesterday, Lorenzo Ruiz, the scribe from Manila who would not deny his faith in Japan. Your line was first of the philippines. Where did you stay yourself? Day one thousand thirty-one.

Angels in the Bible often appear, speak and vanish without giving a name. When Jacob wrestles through the night with the one the prophet Osee later calls an angel, and asks its name, the answer is a question back: why do you ask? So when an angel in scripture does say its name, people pay attention. The Catholic calendar keeps one feast for three of them together: one who fights, one who announces, one who heals. Today's word is what the Church calls them.
screen: `ANGELS WITHOUT NAMES.` → `THREE WHO HAVE THEM.` → `ONE FEAST FOR ALL THREE.`

segments.voice: The word is archangel: a chief angel, one with a particular task. Start with Michael. In the book of Daniel he's a great prince who stands for his people. In the Apocalypse, the book many call Revelation, Michael and his angels fight the dragon. Tradition reads his Hebrew name as a question: who is like God? And there's a small scene in the letter of Jude that shows what that question means. Michael, the archangel, is arguing with the devil over the body of Moses. He could hurl an insult. He doesn't. He says only, in the Douay-Rheims: "The Lord command thee." The warrior angel won't claim the fight as his own. He points past himself. Gabriel is the messenger. He comes to Zechariah in the Temple and to Mary in Nazareth, and when he's doubted, he introduces himself: "I am Gabriel, who stand before God." His job is to carry news, often news that seems impossible. Raphael is the healer and the traveling companion. His story is in the book of Tobias, a book Catholic and Orthodox Christians count as scripture and Protestant churches generally do not. He walks beside young Tobias on a long journey, disguised as an ordinary man, and helps heal Tobias's blind father. Only at the end does he reveal himself: "I am the angel Raphael, one of the seven, who stand before the Lord." A protector, a messenger, a healer. And each one, in the end, points away from himself and toward God.
screen: `MICHAEL: WHO IS LIKE GOD?` · `THE LORD COMMAND THEE.` · `GABRIEL, WHO STANDS BEFORE GOD.` · `RAPHAEL, THE HEALER IN DISGUISE.` · then, large: `EACH POINTS PAST HIMSELF.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Settle and breathe. Some Catholics pray a short prayer to Saint Michael, asking him to defend us in the struggle with evil. If you pray, you can say it now, slowly, or simply ask for protection in your own words, the way Michael did: not by fighting harder, but by handing the fight to God. If you don't pray, bring to mind one battle you're in right now, and notice how much of it you've been trying to win alone. Let it rest for a moment. The bell holds the time.
Archangel. A chief angel with a task: Michael who protects, Gabriel who brings the message, Raphael who heals. Today's word.
Your line: who is like god. Today, when you're tempted to win an argument by insult, try Michael's way: say less, and leave the last word to God. Day one thousand thirty-one.

howItsDone: The feast of Saints Michael, Gabriel and Raphael, archangels, is kept on 29 September; some Catholics pray the Saint Michael prayer, attributed to Pope Leo XIII, at home, and some parishes say it after Mass.

notes: Hook line about angels who vanish without giving a name: confirm framing is fair (canonical text names Michael, Gabriel and Raphael).
Genesis 32:29 paraphrased (the angel answers 'why dost thou ask my name?').
Michael's name as a question 'who is like God?': standard reading; confirm Hebrew spelling and pronunciation.
'The warrior angel' is an interpretive line; Keeper may soften.
Tobias is deuterocanonical: 'Protestant churches generally do not' count it as scripture; confirm phrasing is fair.
Saint Michael prayer described, not quoted, because the English text's translation status is uncertain; howItsDone attributes it to Leo XIII: confirm.
Exact Challoner wording for Jude 1:9 ('The Lord command thee'), Luke 1:19, Tobias 12:15: confirm.

Editor: hook's sweeping 'the Bible is full of' softened to 'often'; Michael's name meaning now framed as 'tradition reads' (claims rule on etymology), in the teach and the original note; howItsDone no longer implies all Catholics pray the Michael prayer after Mass.

Audit: Genesis 32 calls Jacob's opponent 'a man'; the hook now credits Hosea (Osee) 12:4 for calling him an angel. 'Revelation' now named as the Apocalypse first, matching the Douay-Rheims title used on the Catholic path.
